How long does a power station last — hours, or years?

Troubleshooting Updated 2026-08-08

The question splits in two and the answers are unrelated. Over years, the number on the box is a cycle count — 3,000 to 6,000 across the records in this library — and it is only meaningful next to the capacity threshold it was measured to. Two brands here both state 4,000 cycles: one counts down to 80% of original capacity, the other to 70%, so the same number is not the same promise.

Over a single charge the answer is a division, and it needs fields most manufacturers leave out. Only 10 of the 29 station records here state everything that division requires, which is why this site prints an hour figure for that group and refuses to estimate one for the rest.

Open the runtime calculator →

A cycle count without its threshold is not a specification

Three machines, three cycle claims, read with their thresholds

Each pair of rows comes off one manufacturer document. Read them as pairs — a cycle count and the capacity it is counted down to are one statement, and separating them is how "4,000" ends up looking like a fair comparison.

Nothing here is a trick played by any of the three brands: each of them prints its threshold beside its number, and every figure above is off the manufacturer’s own page. The comparison is what goes wrong, because the headline travels and the threshold does not. A machine rated for 4,000 cycles down to 70% has agreed to lose almost a third of its capacity by the end of that count; one rated for the same 4,000 cycles down to 80% has agreed to lose a fifth. Neither will fall over on the day it gets there. A third shape turns up in this library too: a record that states a decade of service life in words and gives no cycle count at all. Years cannot be converted into cycles without knowing how often a machine is cycled, so that record simply has no figure in this column, and no figure is what it gets.

What those counts look like in years, and what the warranty says

Cycles divided by a cycling rate, against the term the maker guarantees

The first two rows are our arithmetic on the counts above, at a deliberately aggressive rate of one full cycle every day. The warranty rows are the manufacturers’ own.

Nobody cycles a backup machine daily, so read this as a floor rather than a forecast.

The record's 6,000 cycles divided by 365 cycles a year. The cycle count is the manufacturer's; the rate is an assumption we state, and the division is ours.

The record's 4,000 cycles divided by the same 365 cycles a year, to the looser 70% threshold. Same arithmetic, same assumption, different endpoint.

Official spec + Derived by WattPair · verified 2026-08-01 · station records · battery block

That gap is the practical finding. Even at a cycling rate no household backup machine will ever see, the cycle counts land two to three times beyond the warranty term — so for anything used a handful of times a year, the cycle number is not the binding constraint and should not be the deciding line on a spec sheet. What it is genuinely useful for is the opposite case: a machine cycled hard every day on a van roof or a balcony, where the count and its threshold start to describe real years.

And the other meaning: how long it lasts on one charge

The same sentence is just as often about a single evening, and that answer is a division rather than a rating: usable capacity, after depth of discharge and inverter efficiency, over the load plus the machine’s own self-consumption. Every one of those four terms has to come from somewhere, and this library holds a complete set for only 10 of the 29 station records. On the rest this site refuses the division rather than filling the gaps with a plausible constant, which is why a runtime figure appears on some records and not on others.

What actually shortens a life, and what does not

The one wear mechanism this library holds hard, dated figures for is temperature: several records publish a charge window narrower than their discharge window, and charging a cold pack outside it is the failure this site would warn about first. Calendar ageing — what a pack loses simply by existing — is not something we hold a figure for, so this page will not put a number on it.

Questions people ask

How long does a power station last?
As a piece of hardware, the manufacturers here rate their packs at 3,000 to 6,000 charge cycles. Divided by one full cycle every day — a rate no household backup unit reaches — that is roughly 8 to 16 years, against warranty terms of 5 to 10 years on the same records. As a single charge, it depends on the load and on the machine’s own self-consumption, and this library holds a complete set for only 10 of the 29 station records.
Is 4,000 cycles better than 3,000?
Not necessarily, because a cycle count is only defined against the capacity it is counted down to. In this library one brand rates 4,000 cycles to 70 percent of original capacity and another rates 4,000 cycles to 80 percent — the second is the stronger claim on the same headline number. Read the threshold before you compare the counts.
When should I replace a power station?
There is no cliff. A pack at its rated cycle count still holds 70 or 80 percent of the capacity it shipped with, depending on which threshold its maker used, and it keeps working past that point with less runtime each year. The practical trigger is the day its remaining capacity stops covering the load you bought it for — which is a question about your loads, not about the battery.
